name: Reiki

lead: Reiki is a Japanese-origin practice in which a practitioner places their hands lightly on, or just above, a person's body in order to channel a "universal energy". It is taken up mainly for relaxation, stress and mood. In looksmaxxing and wellness circles it is occasionally mentioned as part of a calm, recovery-focused routine, with the idea that less stress and better rest show up in skin, sleep and general appearance.

Research has mostly looked at pain, anxiety and mood in clinical groups such as cancer patients and people in palliative care. Some small trials and a 2024 meta-analysis report lower anxiety scores after Reiki, while the US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health says it has not been clearly shown to be effective for any health-related purpose. No study has measured its effect on looks.

paras: A session usually lasts around an hour with the client lying or sitting fully clothed while the practitioner moves through a sequence of hand positions on or just above the body. Practitioners trained at higher levels also offer distance sessions. Sessions are typically booked singly or as a series, and people often combine them with massage, meditation or other relaxation practices.

Reiki involves no ingestion or injection and health agencies report no harmful effects from the sessions themselves. The concern raised by clinicians is that people might delay or replace proven treatment for a serious condition. Practitioner qualifications are not regulated in the US, and session prices vary widely.

angle.text: People use Reiki as a relaxation practice, and some include it in routines aimed at stress and sleep, which they associate with how the skin and face look. The link to appearance is a user-described chain rather than something studied directly.

lead: Reiki is an energy-healing practice developed in Japan in the 1920s by Mikao Usui. Practitioners hold their hands on or a short distance above a client's body, intending to let a universal life energy flow through them to the client. The name combines the Japanese words rei (universal) and ki (vital energy) [1].

People use it mainly for relaxation, stress relief and a sense of well-being. In appearance-focused communities it enters the picture through an explicit chain: stress and poor sleep are commonly discussed as showing up in the face and skin, so practices that promote calm are folded into recovery routines. Reiki has no direct cosmetic effect claimed by its mainstream teachers.

Research has examined Reiki for pain, anxiety, depression and quality of life, usually in small trials. Reviews report mixed and often low-quality results, and the US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH) states that it has not been clearly shown to be effective for any health-related purpose [2]. Studies of appearance outcomes have not been published.
infobox: About 1 hour, clothed, hands on or near the body
US practitioners are not licensed; no central authority for the term

paras: In a typical session the client lies or sits clothed while the practitioner places their hands lightly on or above a series of positions on the body. Practitioners trained to a second level may also work at a distance without contact. Teachers are known as reiki masters, and training is organised in levels [1].

Practitioners describe the process as directing a universal energy so as to support the body's own healing. NCCIH describes it in similar terms, as a complementary approach based on an Eastern belief in such an energy [2].

Mikao Usui founded the practice in Japan in the 1920s and, according to his memorial inscription, taught more than 2,000 people before his death in 1926. His student Chujiro Hayashi passed it on to Hawayo Takata, who opened what is described as the first Reiki clinic in the United States in 1970 [1].

Reiki spread widely through hospitals, hospices and private practice. A 2014 Washington Post report cited by Wikipedia counted at least 60 US hospitals offering it, at prices of roughly $40 to $300 per session, and Cancer Research UK reported in 2019 that some UK cancer centres and hospices offer it free or at low cost [1].

Practitioners say Reiki promotes deep relaxation, reduces pain and anxiety and supports emotional balance. Some wellness writers extend this to sleep quality, mood and a calmer, healthier-looking appearance, drawing on the general idea that stress and sleep loss affect the face and skin. Wikipedia notes that the practice rests on a life-force concept that science has not been able to detect [1].

A 2024 meta-analysis of Reiki for anxiety covering 824 participants reported a significant reduction in anxiety scores compared with controls [3]. A 2019 review of Reiki in palliative care described effects on pain, anxiety, depression and quality of life, while noting that the small number of studies limited firm conclusions [4]. A 2023 systematic review of seven studies in 572 patients with cancer found pain reductions in five of them [5].

Earlier trials include a phase II study of Reiki for pain in advanced cancer patients [6] and a pilot crossover trial of Reiki versus rest for cancer-related fatigue [7]. A 2024 randomised trial in 48 women examined menopausal symptoms and reported lower scores after Reiki [8].

Other reviewers are more cautious. A 2010 best-evidence synthesis of biofield therapies assessed the evidence for Reiki and related practices as limited [9]. NCCIH states that most Reiki research is of low quality with inconsistent results and that Reiki has not been clearly shown to be effective for any health-related purpose [2]. A 2008 systematic review of nine randomised trials, as summarised by Wikipedia, cited small samples and design weaknesses [1]. No published trial has measured skin, facial appearance or physique outcomes.

NCCIH reports that Reiki has not been shown to have harmful effects [2]. The risk most often raised is indirect, namely that a person with a serious condition might replace proven treatment with it [1]. US practitioners are not regulated, certificates can be obtained online, and in 2009 the US Conference of Catholic Bishops advised against Catholic institutions promoting it [1].

Reiki is peripheral to looksmaxxing. It appears mainly in wellness-oriented threads and general forum conversation about alternative practices, where participants discuss it alongside meditation and other recovery habits [10].
